Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

2 include a concise opening that explains how to start a track, adjust listening volume safely, pause playback, and skip to another work, we have not chosen the final device or interface, so do not name a button, menu, app, or headphone model, ask the museum team to insert the approved device directions later, the guide should not promise that audio is available in a language that has not been confirmed, and any mention of additional languages should be a question for staff, please keep operational directions distinct from the interpretive script so they can be updated without rewriting the object tracks, and avoid giving technical instructions that assume visitors own a smartphone

The guide is for visitors moving through the current glass and light galleries, and it should help them notice how objects were made without turning the visit into a lecture. Leave room for people to look up from their headphones, and keep the spoken language welcoming rather than grand or sales-focused. The guide should be useful on a first visit but should not assume that every visitor starts at the entrance. Please make the eventual guide understandable as separate tracks as well as one visit, and do not contact vendors. You may review the existing equipment list and staff notes.

We are planning for a small group of twelve works on the main floor and six works in the upstairs light room. The working inventory uses short object names rather than final label titles, so refer to the blue bowl, the kiln window, the three pane screen, the green bottle, the harbor lamp, and the suspended disc by those names. Do not supply dates, makers, or materials that are not in the notes, and flag a missing fact with a question for the museum team instead of guessing. The main floor route has a narrow doorway beside the blue bowl, and visitors with wheelchairs can use the wider route past the west case. Do not add a second speaker or invent a visitor conversation. The team would like the guide to sound attentive and human while remaining easy to understand in a busy gallery. Suggest plain wording for specialist terms and retain a technical term only when it gives visitors something useful to notice.

Include notes about access and comfort as part of the brief. The upstairs light room has a bench near its entrance, but there is no confirmed seating beside every work. Avoid promising seating throughout the route. Visitors may choose to listen without headphones if the device permits, but the approved device is still unknown. Describe the wider route past the west case accurately, and do not imply that the narrow doorway beside the blue bowl is the only way through. If a track relies on a color distinction, offer a second visible detail where the notes allow it, and do not assume that all visitors have the same vision, hearing, mobility, language background, or amount of time.

The final script should feel like a companion to looking at actual works rather than a substitute for the galleries.
